title: Nandabala's milk
hookLine: after the fasting, a herdsman's daughter gives him milk-rice (Buddhacarita 12)

lines: HE TESTS THE HARD ROAD HIMSELF.
cards: A bowl of rice cooked in milk. Plain food, the kind a grandmother makes for someone who's been sick. In this canto it changes the story.
The prince has left his teachers and gone to live by a river, and now, with no one left to learn from, he tries the one road he hasn't tried: fasting, as hard as a body can bear.
In the penance grove he told the ascetics that pain wasn't the way. Now he tests it on himself.

teach.b: First, the fasting. On the bank of the river Nairanjana, the poem says, he cuts his food down and down, until he lives on almost nothing. His body wastes away.
Some companions, also seeking freedom, settle near him, admiring his discipline and waiting for him to break through. Second, the turn. He doesn't break through.
He breaks down. And he sees why, in paraphrase: this isn't the way to freedom.

teach.h: A STARVED BODY, AN UNSETTLED MIND.
teach.b: A mind can't settle when the body is starving. Calm needs some strength under it. Third, the milk.
He bathes in the river, weak, and comes up out of the water slowly. Then comes Nandabala, the daughter of a chief of the herdsmen, moved by the gods, the poem says, to come to him.
She bows and offers him a bowl of milk-rice. He takes it. He eats.
And strength returns. Fourth, the cost.
His companions watch him eat, decide he has given up, and leave him.
The poem doesn't defend him; it lets the moment be. A woman with a bowl did what no teacher and no hardship could: she gave him back his body, so his mind could do its work.
Other tellings give her a different name, Sujata, and other details; this poem calls her Nandabala.

Look back over the week: a grove that sought heaven through pain, a palace in grief, ministers with every argument, a king with half a kingdom, fire that fuel can't quench, a teacher whose best was not final, and now a bowl of milk-rice, taken with thanks.

how: The offering of milk-rice is remembered in Buddhist art and festivals, and giving food to monks and nuns is a daily practice in some Buddhist communities, where the gift is received as part of the path.

o: an offering poured on a sacred fire
the milk-rice that ends the prince's fast
milk the ascetics drank to win heaven

games.q: by the river: tap the pairs.
p: think he's given up, and leave

s: in this poem, the woman who brings the milk-rice is named Sujata
the poem names her Nandabala; other tellings call her Sujata.
his companions cheer when he eats again
they decide he has given up, and they leave him.
the prince decides a starving body can't settle the mind
calm needs some strength under it, so he accepts the food.

games.q: you've fasted until you can barely stand, and it hasn't brought you closer. a young woman kneels and offers you a bowl of milk-rice. your companions are watching. what do you do?
o: refuse, so they don't think you've quit.
take it, and give it to your companions.
games.why: he eats, and strength returns. his companions decide he has given up and leave him.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you've been going it alone, harder than you need to, and one person who has offered help, or would if you asked.

Picture them holding out a bowl, notice what in you wants to wave it away, and then picture taking it with both hands and saying thank you. Feel what changes in your body when you're not carrying it alone.

wordCard.voice: Nandabala's milk. After fasting brings him no closer, a herdsman's daughter offers the prince milk-rice; he eats, his strength returns, and his companions leave him. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: rice cooked in milk, the dish Nandabala offers.

carryVoice: Your line: strength returns. What's left now is a tree, and the night. Day seven hundred fourteen, done.
